scenarios.title: Turn before the traffic closes
scenarios.objective: Choose a possible turning space while noticing a teammate and opponent ahead.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU carry through the neutral zone toward F2 and D1. F2 occupies your straight path; D1 is closer to the middle. This exercise plans a turn, not a collision or contact play.
cues: D1 is on the middle side.
The positive-y side has room in this freeze.

sources.section: U11 Skills Matrix, printed page 22 (PDF page 22)

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. The U11 matrix includes turning and evasive skating; the model does not demonstrate skate-edge technique or braking distance. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: Which teammate occupies the straight-ahead route from YOU?

options.text: F2
D1
Nobody

questions.explanation: F2 is directly ahead at the same y position. D1 is an opponent offset toward the middle.

questions.prompt: What belongs in this turning decision?

options.text: Room beside the traffic
How much speed and control YOU actually have
The assumption that a teammate cannot obstruct a route

questions.explanation: A useful plan considers both available space and the movement the still picture cannot show.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested controlled-turn plan.

options.text: Notice the traffic before reaching it
Choose a turn you can control
Look again as you leave the turn

questions.explanation: The order is a planning aid. It does not teach a particular edge technique from a static model.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward a possible turning space beside the traffic.
questions.explanation: The example uses the wall-side room short of F2. Another controlled route could work if D1’s movement allows it.

questions.prompt: Suppose F2 moves toward that same outside space. What would help now?

options.text: Keep the planned turn without another look
Reassess space and slow or choose another route
Aim at F2’s original empty spot without checking D1

questions.explanation: Both traffic and available routes changed. Speed control or a different turn can be safer and more useful.

questions.prompt: Why must a turning plan account for a teammate as well as D1?
questions.explanation: A teammate can occupy the route even without defending it. Explain how you would preserve room for both players.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate before turning?

options.text: F2 is ahead; I am checking the side space around D1
The outside lane is mine even if the picture changes
D1 does not affect the turn

questions.explanation: The call identifies both traffic cues and leaves the turn adaptable.

questions.prompt: Which two changes would make the first turn poor?

options.text: F2 moves into the side space
D1 closes the turn lane
YOU still sees the puck

questions.explanation: The teammate and defender can remove the turn; puck visibility alone is not enough.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a side-space entry that avoids F2 and D1.
questions.explanation: This point changes the turn angle while leaving both players visible.

questions.prompt: F2 enters the side space as you begin turning. Explain your adjustment.
questions.explanation: Do not crowd F2. Protect the puck, choose another angle, and re-check D1 before continuing.

scenarios.title: Receive into an open shoulder
scenarios.objective: Plan a receiving destination while separating a future pass from current possession.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. F1 is preparing a pass across the neutral zone to YOU. D1 waits up ice on your middle-side shoulder. The pass has not left F1’s stick.
cues: D1 is beyond the receiver toward the attacking end.
Space is available farther toward the negative-y wall.

sources.section: U11 Skills Matrix, printed page 22 (PDF page 22)

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. Moving reception is an age-topic connection. Handedness and actual pass speed are not represented. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: Which player is up ice of YOU, closer to the right net?

options.text: F1
D1
Both F1 and D1

questions.explanation: D1 is at x=8, YOU at x=4 and F1 at x=-2.

questions.prompt: What would you check when choosing where to receive?

options.text: A usable line from F1
Room for the next action after the touch
Only which spot is closest to the right net

questions.explanation: Reception needs both an incoming line and options afterward. Being farther forward alone does not settle it.

questions.prompt: Order this suggested reception routine.

options.text: Offer a target in available space
Control the incoming puck
Read D1 before the next pass or carry

questions.explanation: This teaching order separates receiving from the next action; a skilled one-touch play would require different timing evidence.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward a receiving point with room away from D1.
questions.explanation: The sample moves toward the side boards away from D1 while retaining a diagonal pass from F1. It is not the only receiving point.

questions.prompt: If the pass reaches behind YOU instead of the intended spot, what should the plan account for?

options.text: The actual puck location before the next action
Only the original target point
An automatic shot before possession

questions.explanation: A misplaced pass changes the task. Regain control or adjust before assuming the planned continuation.

questions.prompt: What could make receiving slightly wider useful in this picture?
questions.explanation: Connect the receiving line, D1’s position and the next available action. Wider is not always better if it closes another option.

questions.prompt: What should F1 know about your receiving target?

options.text: The wider target is available only while D1 stays inside it
I will turn up ice before locating the arriving puck
Keep aiming at my old spot if I move wider

questions.explanation: The message ties the target to D1 and F1's route, keeping the choice conditional.

questions.prompt: Which two details support the wider reception?

options.text: F1 can reach the diagonal target
D1 is not closing it yet
YOU have already chosen the next touch before checking the arrival

questions.explanation: The passer and defender cues make the target usable; the next touch still needs a scan.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a wider receiving point on the neutral-zone side of D1.
questions.explanation: The point is on the neutral-zone side of D1 and opens F1's diagonal lane; the receiving choice still depends on the actual pressure.

questions.prompt: The puck arrives behind YOU. What do you say and do?
questions.explanation: Call the miss, recover the actual puck under control, and name whether D1 or F1 changes the next option.

scenarios.title: Use the half wall to change the passing route
scenarios.objective: Distinguish a blocked direct line from an unproven indirect wall option.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. F1 has the puck near the half wall, the side-board area partway into the attacking zone. D1 stands directly between F1 and YOU. Consider an indirect pass using the boards; no bounce has been simulated.
cues: D1 blocks the straight F1-to-YOU line.
The side boards offer a different possible route.
D2 remains nearer the middle and goal.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. The manual includes indirect passing. Board rebound angle, speed and interception are not validated. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: What makes the direct half-wall pass difficult in this freeze?

options.text: D2 is the current puck carrier
D1 is between F1 and YOU
YOU are the puck carrier

questions.explanation: D1 lies on the direct line between the carrier and receiver.

questions.prompt: Which details matter before trying an indirect wall pass?

options.text: Where the puck might leave the boards
Whether YOU can reach its exit path
Whether the puck is guaranteed to bounce as planned

questions.explanation: The indirect route needs a reachable exit and control. A drawing alone does not prove the bounce.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested wall-pass planning routine.

options.text: Notice the blocked direct line
Agree on a possible board route and receiving area
Read the actual rebound before the next touch

questions.explanation: This is an original planning example; the puck must actually rebound into reachable space.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward a possible receiving area along the half wall.
questions.explanation: The sample is closer to a board-pass exit and outside D1’s current position. Other angles may be better with real puck speed.

questions.prompt: Suppose D1 turns toward the boards before F1 releases. What should F1 and YOU revisit?

options.text: Whether that wall route remains open
Only how the direct route looked before D1 moved
A rule that every blocked pass must use the wall

questions.explanation: The defender can close the indirect route too. Another support angle or hold may be useful.

questions.prompt: How is using the half wall different from simply passing through D1?
questions.explanation: Describe the changed puck path and the new receiving information it requires. Do not assume a successful bounce.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate before the wall option?

options.text: D1 blocks the direct lane; watch the rebound near the wall
Aim at the same board spot even if I move
Use the direct pass before checking D1’s stick

questions.explanation: The message names D1 and the rebound, explaining why the route needs another read.

questions.prompt: Which two cues shape the bank point?

options.text: Where YOU can receive the rebound
Whether D2 remains available at the opposite point
That D2 does not move

questions.explanation: The rebound location and D2’s opposite-point support determine whether the wall changes the useful route; D2’s stillness alone does not.

questions.prompt: Move YOU farther along the wall beyond D1.
questions.explanation: This point presents a changed wall relationship beyond D1 while keeping D2 visible for the next scan.

questions.prompt: D1 turns to the wall before the pass. Explain what you recheck.
questions.explanation: Compare the rebound route with D2’s opposite-point support and D1’s new facing. Use whichever remains reachable and protected.

scenarios.title: Recover the pass that missed
scenarios.objective: Update a receiving plan after the puck goes beyond the intended target.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. F1’s pass has missed YOU’s stick and the puck is now loose toward the side boards. D1 is farther inside. The scene begins after the missed reception.
cues: YOU do not currently own the puck.
The loose puck is wider than YOU.
The original receiving spot is no longer the puck location.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. The miss is stated, not animated. No blame or technique diagnosis can be inferred from this scene. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: Which point should the recovery plan respond to?

options.text: The loose puck’s current location
Only YOU’s old receiving spot
F1’s position before the pass

questions.explanation: The actual puck is at the new loose location, not the planned receiving point.

questions.prompt: Which questions would help YOU recover usefully?

options.text: Can I reach the puck under control?
Where can D1 apply pressure?
Must I repeat the exact intended first touch?

questions.explanation: The useful plan depends on current access and pressure, rather than repeating a touch that did not happen.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested response to the missed pass.

options.text: Locate the puck after the miss
Approach with awareness of D1
Choose the next action once control is available

questions.explanation: A miss creates a new read. This is a recovery suggestion, not a judgment of the receiver’s ability.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to show an approach toward the actual loose puck.
questions.explanation: The sample moves toward the puck while remaining short of it. Arrival time and control still need real movement.

questions.prompt: If D1 reaches the puck first, what has changed?

options.text: YOU remain the carrier because the pass was intended for you
The next read becomes defending or regaining possession
F1’s original pass must be replayed

questions.explanation: Actual possession controls the next situation; the intended receiver does not retain ownership after an opponent recovers.

questions.prompt: What would you say to F1 after this miss to help the next play?
questions.explanation: Describe useful information or support rather than blame. Explain what you need to see from D1 or F1 next.

questions.prompt: What should YOU tell F1 after the pass drifts?

options.text: The puck is below me; I am checking D1 before recovering
The intended target is still the puck
D1 does not reach it

questions.explanation: The call reports the actual puck and pressure, which replaces the planned target.

questions.prompt: Which two facts change the recovery route?

options.text: D1’s distance from the loose puck
Whether YOU can arrive with control
F1’s original intention alone

questions.explanation: Live pressure and whether YOU can arrive with control matter after a miss; F1’s original intention does not locate the puck.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the loose puck on the far-side lane from F1's intended pass.
questions.explanation: This point approaches the actual puck from the far-side lane of F1's intended pass while preserving a view of D1; arrival and control remain open.

questions.prompt: D1 arrives first. How do you communicate the new job?
questions.explanation: Say D1 has possession, then identify whether to pressure D1 or support F1 while F1 and YOU re-form.

scenarios.title: A defender in the slot shooting line
scenarios.objective: Relate a shooting lane through the slot to a separate half-wall passing option.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU own the puck in the high slot, the middle area farther from the net. D1 stands in the direct shooting line. F2 is near the half wall. The goalie is squarely near the goal centre.
cues: D1 lies between YOU and the goal.
F2 supplies a different passing angle at the half wall.
A visible lane obstruction does not reveal save probability.

options.text: D1’s stick/body line

options.text: Identify the blocker and the support option
Choose a controlled action supported by those cues
Read the defence again after the puck moves

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward a possible shooting angle away from D1’s current line.
questions.explanation: The example changes the angle without moving D1 or the goalie. It does not certify an open net or a reachable move.

questions.prompt: If D1 moves toward F2 and the direct lane clears, what becomes worth reconsidering?

options.text: A controlled shot through the newly available lane
Only a pass to the same half-wall spot
Shooting without checking the changed pressure

questions.explanation: A changed blocker can make a shot more plausible. Control, pressure and the goalie still matter.

questions.prompt: Why might the slot and half wall offer different choices on this play?
questions.explanation: Name the goal line, blocker and passing angle. A location name helps describe space but does not by itself decide the action.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call when D1 moves toward F2?

options.text: The lane may be open; check the net and F2 before choosing
The shot is certain
F2 is no longer part of the play

questions.explanation: The call connects D1's movement to the newly changed lane without promising an outcome.

questions.prompt: Which two checks belong before using the opening?

options.text: Whether the shooting lane stays clear
Whether F2 offers a safer reachable pass
That D1 moved once

questions.explanation: The lane and support must both be checked after D1 moves.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a slight outside shooting angle with F2 visible.

questions.prompt: D1 leaves the lane but F2 is covered. What is your next read?
questions.explanation: The opening may support a shot or protected touch, but check the net-side space and D1's recovery before deciding.
